title: CPU Performance and the Iron Law
summary: CPU time = Instruction Count × CPI × Clock Cycle Time — the "Iron Law" of processor performance, splitting speed into three independently movable levers (the ISA/compiler, the microarchitecture, and the silicon) that every design decision in this discipline trades off against.

references.label: Cornell CS3410 — Pipelining & Performance Notes
Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition

title: Why Pipeline: Latency vs. Throughput
summary: The single-cycle CPU already built in Digital Logic & Computer Organization is correct but wasteful — every instruction's clock cycle must be as long as the slowest instruction ever needs. Pipelining overlaps instructions in flight, trading a longer per-instruction latency for a dramatically higher throughput.

references.label: MIT 6.004 — Pipelining the Beta
Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition

title: The 5-Stage RISC Pipeline: IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB

related.label: The Datapath: Registers, ALU, and Buses

summary: Splitting the single-cycle datapath at five natural points — Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Write-Back — with a pipeline register latching state between each stage, so five different instructions can occupy the five stages simultaneously, one cycle apart.

references.label: Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition
MIT 6.004 — Pipelining the Beta

title: Structural Hazards
summary: Two instructions in different stages want the same physical resource in the same cycle — classically, one instruction's Fetch and another's Memory access both wanting the one memory port — resolved in real designs by giving instructions and data their own separate caches.

references.label: Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition
Berkeley CS61C — Great Ideas in Computer Architecture

title: Data Hazards and Forwarding
summary: A register written by one instruction is read by the very next one before the write has actually reached the register file — a read-after-write hazard fixed not by waiting, but by forwarding the not-yet-written-back result directly into the dependent instruction's ALU input.

references.label: Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition

title: The Load-Use Hazard and Pipeline Stalls
summary: One data hazard forwarding cannot fully erase: a load's value isn't available until after the Memory stage, so an immediately-dependent instruction still needs one bubble cycle — a stall that a smart compiler can often hide entirely by reordering independent instructions into that gap.

references.label: Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition
Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)

title: Control Hazards and Branch Penalties
summary: A branch's taken/not-taken outcome isn't known until well after the next instructions have already been fetched — naively flushing the pipeline on every branch costs real, quantifiable cycles, and is the exact problem branch prediction exists to reduce.

references.label: Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition
MIT 6.004 — Pipelining the Beta

title: Branch Prediction
summary: Guessing a branch's outcome before it's known — static prediction (always/backward-taken), and dynamic prediction with a branch history table of 1-bit or 2-bit saturating counters — turns most branch penalties into the common case of a correct guess instead of a guaranteed stall.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
Berkeley CS61C — Great Ideas in Computer Architecture

title: Speculative and Out-of-Order Execution
summary: Executing past a predicted branch before its outcome is confirmed, and letting independent instructions issue out of program order around one that's stalled — covered here only at the concept level (what problem it solves and what a misprediction rollback costs), with the full mechanics (reorder buffers, Tomasulo-style scheduling) left to a more advanced course.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition

title: The Memory Hierarchy and Locality
summary: A pyramid of storage technologies — registers, on-chip cache, main memory, disk — trading capacity for speed at every level; temporal and spatial locality are the empirical properties of real programs that let a small, fast cache behave, most of the time, as if all of memory were that fast.

references.label: Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture

title: Cache Organization: Blocks, Tags, and Direct Mapping
summary: An address splits into a tag, an index, and a block offset; a direct-mapped cache uses the index to pick exactly one slot per address and the tag to check whether the resident block is actually the one being asked for.

references.label: CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture
Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)

title: Set-Associative and Fully Associative Caches
summary: Relaxing direct mapping's one-slot-per-address rigidity to N possible slots ("ways") per set trades extra comparison hardware for far fewer conflict misses; a fully associative cache is the limiting case of one giant set with every line a candidate.

references.label: CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture
Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)

title: Cache Replacement Policies
summary: When a set is full and a new block must be brought in, something has to be evicted — least-recently-used (and its cheaper hardware approximations), FIFO, and random are the real policies in use, each a different bet on which resident line is least likely to be reused soon.

references.label: Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture

title: Write Policies: Write-Through and Write-Back
summary: A write can either update main memory immediately every time (write-through) or only mark the line dirty and defer the update until it's evicted (write-back) — paired with write-allocate/no-write-allocate for what happens on a write miss; this exact dirty-line bookkeeping is what a multicore coherence protocol later has to generalize across several caches at once.

references.label: Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture

title: Average Memory Access Time and Multilevel Caches
summary: AMAT = Hit Time + Miss Rate × Miss Penalty, applied recursively across a real L1/L2/L3/DRAM hierarchy with representative latency numbers — the single formula this whole cluster has been building toward, and the one CS2013 names directly as a required computational skill.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)

title: Cache-Friendly Code and Locality in Practice
summary: Row-major traversal order and cache blocking (tiling) turn everything in this cluster into a measurable, real-world effect: the same algorithm, the same asymptotic complexity, and a dramatically different wall-clock time depending only on the order memory is touched.

references.label: Bryant & O'Hallaron — Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (CS:APP)
CMU 15-213 — Cache Memories Lecture

title: Why Multicore: The Power Wall and the End of Free Frequency Scaling
summary: Around 2004-2005, chipmakers hit a real physical wall: Pollack's Rule (performance scales only with the square root of added logic, while power scales linearly with it) made single-core designs increasingly power-inefficient, prompting the industry-wide pivot to multiple simpler cores — the historical turn Herb Sutter named "the free lunch is over" for software.

references.label: Herb Sutter — The Free Lunch Is Over
Cambridge ACS — Performance Prediction: Pollack's Rule

title: Multicore Architectures and Shared Memory
summary: A typical multicore chip gives each core its own private L1 (and often L2) cache but shares one L3 and one main memory across all of them — a layout that immediately raises a new correctness question this discipline hasn't had to face yet: what happens when two cores cache the same line?

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
CMU 15-418 — Snooping Cache Coherence Lecture

title: Cache Coherence and the MESI Protocol
summary: The coherence problem, precisely stated: every core must eventually observe every write to a shared line, in some consistent order. MESI's four per-line states — Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid — and the snooped bus messages between them are the standard protocol real multicore chips use to guarantee exactly that.

references.label: CMU 15-418 — Snooping Cache Coherence Lecture
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area

title: False Sharing
summary: Two threads touching two completely unrelated variables can still fight over the same cache line if those variables happen to land in it — MESI keeps the data correct, but the line ping-pongs Modified/Invalid between cores on every access, turning a correctness protocol into a real, measurable performance bug.

references.label: CoffeeBeforeArch — Performance Implications of False Sharing
CMU 15-418 — Snooping Cache Coherence Lecture

title: Flynn's Taxonomy and SIMD
summary: Flynn's classification of machines by instruction and data streams — SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD — places the multicore chip just covered squarely in MIMD (many independent instruction streams); SIMD is the different axis this cluster turns to next: one instruction stream driving many data lanes at once.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
Harris & Harris — Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition

title: GPU Architecture and the SIMT Execution Model
summary: A GPU packs thousands of simple lanes into streaming multiprocessors, executing groups of 32 threads (a warp) in lockstep under SIMT — SIMD's more flexible cousin, which lets individual threads take different branches at the cost of serializing the divergent paths. Scoped to the hardware execution model only; the CUDA/OpenCL programming model belongs to `systems/parallel-computing`.

references.label: NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide — Advanced Kernel Programming (SIMT/Warps)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area

title: Capstone: The Memory and Power Walls — A History of Tradeoffs
summary: Three real historical walls, tied together: the ILP wall (speculation and out-of-order issue ran out of independent work to exploit), the memory wall (AMAT increasingly dominated by DRAM latency no cache level fully hides), and the power wall (Pollack's Rule) — the same three forces that ended the single-core "free lunch" and made pipelining depth, cache hierarchy, multicore, and SIMD/GPU architecture the four real answers this discipline covered, in the order it covered them.

references.label: Herb Sutter — The Free Lunch Is Over
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Architecture and Organization Knowledge Area
